channel.title: ResearchBuzz - Transformed
channel.description: News and resources covering social media, search engines, databases, archives, and other such information collections. Since 1998.

item.title: Amazon, Walmart AI detect ‘made in USA’ fraud but do not flag it, study says
item.description: Reuters: “Amazon and Walmart AI shopping assistants can often detect ‌when “Made in USA” product labels are false, but the big retailers are not using that technology to crack down on the listings, according to a new study, opens new tab from a think tank led by former Chair of the U.S. Federal Trade Commission Lina Khan. The study resurfaces ​questions about AI shopping assistants’ mixed incentives, as retailers see the technology as a way to boost spending.”

item.title: A data centre is uniting bugs and bikers to fight Google: ‘We demand you replace what you destroy’
item.description: The Big Issue: “[Mark] Sexton is a member of the Thurrock Hammers, a speedway club whose members love tearing around a shale oval circuit on methanol-powered 500 cc motorcycles with no brakes. Buglife are conservationists obsessed with halting invertebrate extinction. Under normal circumstances, a live-and-let-live relationship might be the best they could hope for.”

item.title: New Poll: Voter Opposition To Local AI Data Centers Hits High Amid Rising Utility Concerns
item.description: Tampa Free Press: “Public opposition to building artificial intelligence data centers in local communities has reached its highest level in ten months, according to newly released survey tracking data from Morning Consult. For the first time since November, support for banning nearby data center construction outpolled opposition, with 45 percent of voters favoring local bans.”

item.title: EU lays out $11.4 billion for 7 AI gigafactories as it aims to catch up with US and China
item.description: Associated Press: “The European Union is offering 10 billion euros ($11.4 billion) in funding for firms to erect seven AI gigafactories as it seeks to close the AI gap with U.S. and China, the 27-nation bloc’s executive said on Thursday. The European Commission said it would like the public financing to draw an additional 20 billion euros ($22.8 billion) in private investment.”

item.title: Data center approvals in Texas halted until audits completed, Gov. Greg Abbott says
item.description: Texas Tribune: “Amid growing public backlash to the rapid buildout of data centers across Texas, Gov. Greg Abbott on Monday announced a moratorium on the approval of data centers until regulatory agencies can audit proposed data centers seeking connection to the state’s electric grid.”

item.title: As AI glasses get harder to detect, universities scramble to update exam rules
item.description: Korea Times: “Artificial intelligence (AI) glasses are emerging as a new tool for academic dishonesty, with a string of recent cases exposing their potential for misuse, putting the education sector under growing pressure to respond.”

item.title: Senate committee looks to stop AI-enabled fraud against older adults
item.description: Spectrum News: “Older adults shared harrowing stories of AI-enabled scams they experienced and the difficulties they encountered to resolve them during a Senate Special Committee on Aging hearing Wednesday about deepfakes, chatbots and senior fraud. The bipartisan committee is seeking ways to safeguard older Americans from AI-enabled fraud that is projected to reach $40 billion in the United States next year.”

item.title: ChatGPT dominates early AI spending in Congress as lawmakers weigh regulation
item.description: CNBC: “OpenAI is dominating the first visible wave of artificial intelligence spending inside Congress. The maker of ChatGPT accounted for roughly $9 out of every $10 spent on identifiable AI tools by House offices, committees and institutional accounts during the year ending March 31, according to a CNBC analysis of House disbursement records.”

item.title: A record-breaking eight Pulitzer awardees disclosed AI use this year
item.description: NiemanLab: “For the past two years, I’ve spoken to Pulitzer-recognized reporters about how they used AI in their reporting. Both years, generative AI took a back seat to more conventional machine learning technologies, like using embedding models to produce complex data visualizations and pattern recognition models to analyze satellite imagery in conflict zones. This year, though, generative AI tools and commercial large language models (LLMs) were more commonly used, largely to speed up the process of combing through document dumps.”

item.title: Larry Ellison Bet It All on the A.I. Boom. Will He Be the Face of the A.I. Bubble?
item.description: New York Times: This link goes to a gift article. “Ellison, who was 80 and worth in the neighborhood of $200 billion, had an appointment at the White House. He didn’t bother to take a driver’s license — he needed to call someone on the president’s staff to vouch for him at the gate — but there he was, at 2 p.m., standing beside Donald Trump in the Roosevelt Room as the president announced ‘the largest A.I. infrastructure project by far in history’ and told the world that his friend Larry Ellison was just the man to get it done.”

item.title: Influencers draw backlash for attending OpenAI’s first luxury trip
item.description: TechCrunch: “Another influencer who posted about the trip was asked if she was going to do a get-ready-with-me (the popular video format where influencers record their process of getting ready) about touring a data center. When TechCrunch reached out to a third influencer about her time on the trip, she appeared to have deleted the video she made about her time there, although she retained others that don’t explicitly reference that they were part of the OpenAI brand trip.”

item.title: How do we prevent AI agents from going rogue? It starts with a new kind of measurement
item.description: The Guardian: “Ask a modern AI agent to save money on your phone plan and it might simply cancel the plan. Tell it to book a flight, and it might hack the airline website to override restrictions. Or, like OpenAI, ask it to do well on a test and it might break into another company to steal the answers. Each time, it recognizably completed the task you set, but it didn’t do what you would have wanted.”

item.title: OpenAI will provide free AI models to select researchers
item.description: Engadget: “OpenAI is launching a new program called ChatGPT for Academic Researchers that will offer free access to the company’s AI models to 100,000 scientists, mathematicians and engineers. Researchers from ‘select academic institutions’ included in the program will receive hands-on support from OpenAI, access to the company’s latest GPT-5.6 Sol Pro model and be able to invite four collaborators from their institution to participate.”

item.title: Want to Fight Back Against Big Tech? Start Here.
item.description: New York Times: This link goes to a gift article. “All of the speculation and hype around A.I. is hiding the fact that the technology isn’t just large language models or agents or data centers. It is the backbone of a superstructure that merges regressive politics with unchecked economic power in the guise of technological innovation. Put simply, there is too much money, some of it too untraceable, giving a small group of unelected people too much power over the people. That’s data politics.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: The best headphone upgrade I got this year cost absolutely nothing
item.description: MakeUseOf: “I’m always looking to find ways to make my headphones and earbuds sound better. Better still, I find ways to make them sound better for free. And this time out, I’ve found the golden ticket: AutoEQ. It’s a database filled with detailed frequency responses for popular headphone and earbud models compiled by leading sources such as oratory1990, Crinacle, Innerfidelity, and Rtings, all leading voices in EQ design. In short, you take the custom-designed EQ, copy it into a suitable EQ app, and off you go; your music sounds better instantly.”

item.title: Australia hikes levy for tech giants that fail to strike local news deals
item.description: Reuters: “The Australian government has hiked a planned levy that will force tech giants to pay multimillion-dollar charges ​if they fail to strike commercial deals with local ‌media outlets for news on their platforms.”

item.title: Hihōkan: Japan’s Vanishing Roadside Sex Museums, and the Tokyo Bar Keeping Them Alive
item.description: Unseen Japan: “Japan gets a lot of attention for its annual fertility festivals, such as the Kanamara Matsuri (Festival of the Steel Phallus – ouch). A lesser-known phenomenon, though, is the ���宝館 (hihōkan), or roadside sex museums. Unfortunately, there’s a reason you don’t hear much about them. Outside of two remaining installations, most have died off. Fortunately, there’s still a spot in Tokyo that’s dedicated to keeping this collision between sex and kitsch alive in the 21st century.”

item.title: Bluesky’s new CEO wants a big tent, not a bubble
item.description: The Verge: “Toni was formerly the CEO of Automattic, which makes the huge WordPress web content management platform, and you’ll hear him make the case that this period in social networking feels a lot like the early days of the web, and that success looks like a vibrant ecosystem with lots of big players that might take a decade to fully develop.”

item.title: Feds face multistate lawsuit over bid to release low-income assistance records
item.description: Courthouse News Network: “A coalition of 24 states and Washington, D.C. sued the Trump administration on Monday, challenging a decision authorizing the disclosure of personal information for individuals participating in the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families program. According to the coalition, the Administration for Children and Families issued a notice on June 23 that it would begin releasing such information to any private or public entity the administration chooses starting August 11, to scrutinize blue states’ compliance with the assistance program’s statutory requirements.”

item.title: Russians who film Ukrainian attacks and post them on social media are being detained, fined, and forced to apologize on camera
item.description: Meduza: “Most regional administrations in Russia have already banned filming of strikes and their aftermath, but Russians keep posting footage of fires and flying missiles on social media. Mediazona reports on what this has meant for some of them. Meduza is publishing the article in full.”

item.title: Australian watchdog files legal action against Telegram, saying it failed to remove violent content
item.description: Associated Press: “Australia’s online safety watchdog has filed legal action against messaging app Telegram, saying the platform failed to remove extremist content including videos of white supremacist mass shootings in Buffalo, New York, and the New Zealand city of Christchurch as well as Islamic State group beheadings.”

item.title: ‘Fortnite on steroids’: the virtual gaming worlds transformed to train British soldiers
item.description: The Guardian: “Modern armies have been training in virtual environments for decades. In 2002, the US army launched a video game called America’s Army, initially run on Windows, a multiplayer shooting scenario that aimed to model combat situations but was criticised as being propaganda for the US military. A new generation of companies are trying to offer something different: intricate, layered models of systems or places that can capture the second-order consequences of events.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: Motorola Launches Indigenous Collections App to Help Preserve Ojibwe Language and Culture
item.description: Native News Online: “The free Android app, which will be available through the Google Play Store, is designed to support Indigenous language and cultural revitalization by bringing together traditional stories, geographic landmarks, family history, and key vocabulary in a single platform. The app aims to help users understand not only Ojibwe words but also the cultural teachings and meanings embedded within them.”

item.title: FBI investigates as Michigan joins Minnesota in reporting cyberattacks on its water systems
item.description: Associated Press: “Michigan on Saturday joined Minnesota in reporting cyberattacks on nine of the state’s water systems but an official said all systems were operating ‘safely.’ Earlier this week, authorities said cyberattacks targeted over 30 water systems in Minnesota. The source of the attacks is being investigated, but they came amid warnings that Iranian hackers have been focused on such systems.”

item.title: Is Myspace coming back? Owners confirm relaunch plans
item.description: Mashable: “Chris and Tim Vanderhook, whose company acquired Myspace in 2011, say they plan to relaunch the once-dominant social media platform. The brothers confirmed their intentions in Tommy Avallone’s recent documentary Myspace, although they have not announced when the relaunch will happen or what it will look like.”

item.title: These 4 Adobe alternatives are so good now, I’m confused why anyone still subscribes
item.description: MakeUseOf: “For decades, Adobe has created a range of apps and tools that have become industry standards for design, editing, documentation, and more. While there are very few exceptions, most of these Adobe tools are so expensive that most of us cannot afford them. Fortunately, there’s no dearth of free and often open-source alternatives to these tools, offering similar, if not better, features.”

item.title: Bandcamp Has A Spam Problem
item.description: Doc Pop: “Spammers are registering unclaimed Bandcamp usernames for artists like The Murder City Devils, Shudder to Think, and DJ Spooky. The spammers then claim that band’s URL (ie ‘DJSpooky.Bandcamp.com’) and use it to drive traffic to scam sites like ‘booop.lol/2e29’, which then asks the user for a credit card in order to download the album.”

item.title: You Don’t Want Smart Glasses That Record Everything You Say—Trust Me
item.description: Gizmodo: “The $399 MemoMind One are camera-less smart glasses with a monochrome display, microphones, and speakers. On paper, they’re a lot like the Even G2 made by Even Realities, which are also camera-less and focus more on productivity and notifications than entertainment, but there’s one major difference.”

item.title: ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Is X’s Latest Bootleg Leak, Gets Millions Of Views Before Taken Down
item.description: Deadline: “As Tom Holland’s summer blockbusters take over the big screen, X has spoiled yet another one of the actor’s theatrical releases. Following the leak of a high-quality bootleg of The Odyssey on X last week, Spider-Man: Brand New Day was leaked Friday morning on the Elon Musk-owned social media platform, with the movie reaching millions of accounts before it was taken down later that day. Deadline has reached out to Sony for comment.”

item.title: South Korea wrote a fact-checking code into law. Korean fact-checkers are wary.
item.description: Poynter: “In South Korea, anyone who believes an online post is false can now report it. The company that hosts the post must then decide whether the complaint is valid. That is how an amendment to the Network Act, which took effect July 7, is designed to work. It applies to nine platforms with at least a million daily users, among them Naver, Kakao, Google, Meta and TikTok.”

item.title: Reddit keeps its strange DMCA fight over Google search results alive
item.description: Ars Technica: “On Friday, a judge largely denied a motion to dismiss from a web scraper, SerpApi, which is accused of conspiring with Perplexity AI to illegally scrape copyrighted Reddit content from Google search results.”

item.title: Nvidia behind $50 billion lease on Texas data center, FT reports
item.description: Reuters: “Nvidia has signed leases worth up to $50 ​billion for Hut 8’s (HUT.O), opens new tab Texas data center, the ‌Financial Times reported on Tuesday, citing five people familiar with the deal. Hut 8 said last week its 1-gigawatt Beacon Point ​campus had a base-term contract value of $19.6 billion ​over 15 years, rising to as much as $50.2 ⁠billion if renewal options are exercised.”

item.title: Study shows excessive time online is associated with stress, bad moods, and abandoning enjoyable activities
item.description: TechSpot: “Those with more severe problematic internet use reported worse moods, greater stress, longer usage times, and more neglect of other parts of their lives. The strongest predictor of whether someone would engage in their designated activity on a given day wasn’t stress or mood but temptation.”

item.title: Let’s play: Designing the preservation of video games
item.description: NFSA: “Video games are more than art; they are culture. Games are for entertainment, stimulation and challenge, but increasingly for social connection, mental health, motivation, education and training. We’re not talking about teenage boys locked in their bedrooms shooting aliens anymore: over a decade, the average age of a gamer in Australia has risen from under 25 to 35 years of age.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: New Gaming Accessibility Hub Launches as the Largest Centralized Database for Inclusive Gaming Resources and Includes Misophonia
item.description: Misophonia International: “Despite significant industry advancements in recent years, finding tailored accessibility information—such as specific controller remapping options, visual assistance mods, or audio cue guides—often requires sifting through scattered forums, developer notes, and community wikis. GamingAccessibility.org simplifies this process by bringing hardware solutions, software utilities, platform guidelines, and community-driven modifications into a single, intuitive directory.”

item.title: Your phone can 3D-scan a real object well enough to print a copy of it (for free)
item.description: MakeUseOf: “Knowing how to model a part in CAD or 3D design software is one thing, but no matter how skilled you are, if you’re working with a particularly complex part, it can take a lot of time and effort, even if Claude is helping you make 3D parts. The alternative is to 3D scan whatever it is you need to design and work from that. However, 3D scanners can be costly. So if you don’t want to drop $2000 on a laser scanner or dedicated LiDAR rig, your phone’s cameras might just do the trick.”

item.title: Is the Internet panopticon going to ruin live music too?
item.description: Chicago Reader: “Our experience of culture is shaped by social media, streaming services, and other Web-based platforms that mine our data (and may eventually send us $35 checks after settling a class-action lawsuit). But how do those platforms influence how we experience live music? Spotify famously collects vast troves of data, only some of which it ever shares with users or artists—what effect does that have on the concerts we might see in person? As near as anyone can tell, very little.”

item.title: Can Winamp Ride the Retro Tech Wave All the Way Onto Spotify’s Private Beach?
item.description: Gizmodo: “This week brought the news that Winamp—remember Winamp?—is planning to relaunch next year as a sort of one-player-for-everything app, with an integrated streaming service provided by French company Deezer along with the capability to play music from ‘users’ local music libraries, internet radio stations, podcasts, personal cloud-based collections and other audio sources.'”

item.title: Bluesky Says Kremlin Is Hacking Its Platform to Spread Propaganda
item.description: New York Times: This link goes to a gift article. “The campaign, which the researchers at Clemson linked to the Social Design Agency, a company in Moscow, shows how Russia continues to seek new ways to erode public support for Ukraine, which Russian forces invaded in 2022. Bluesky has grown more prominent as a rival platform to X since X’s owner, Elon Musk, threw his political support behind President Trump before the 2024 election. With 42 million users, though, Bluesky trails far behind X’s nearly 600 million.”

item.title: 70 years of St. Louis history is stuck in a Denver data center, PBS station claims
item.description: Denver Post: “A St. Louis PBS station says its 70-year archive of programming is stuck in a Denver data center after a cloud storage company cut off the TV station’s access to the 50 terabytes of data this spring. Nine PBS filed a lawsuit Tuesday in Denver District Court seeking the safe return of the data, which the station’s attorneys believe is being stored within Iron Mountain Data Centers DEN-1, a data center at 4300 Brighton Road in north Denver.”

item.title: Iran struck Amazon data centers again amid widening war, satellites show
item.description: Ars Technica: “Satellite images have revealed new damage to Amazon data centers in the Middle East along with at least one crucial Saudi oil facility, following missile and drone attacks by Iran and its Houthi allies. The images from Europe’s Copernicus Sentinel-2 satellites provide evidence of a widening war as the United States and several Gulf states exchange military strikes with Iran, the Houthi faction in Yemen, and Iran-backed militias in Iraq.”

item.title: Hokkaido University Apologizes for a Century of Ainu Remains Research
item.description: Unseen Japan: “On July 27, 2026, Hokkaido University issued its first-ever proper apology for a prewar research program. The medical school collected and studied more than 1,000 sets of Ainu remains. The university expressed that the work ‘deeply wounded the dignity of the Ainu people.'”

item.title: Kirstin Downey: Hawaiʻi’s Historic Sites Are At Risk As Regulations Crumble
item.description: Honolulu Civil Beat: “Native Hawaiian sites may be among those at risk, historic preservation experts said Thursday at a webinar organized by the National Trust for Historic Preservation because, like tribal lands, supporters seek to protect not just historic buildings but also historic or sacred landscapes. The federal government owns about one-fifth of the land in Hawaiʻi and its construction projects have sweeping consequences.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: Tinder Pauses AI Photo Editing Tool After Woman Creeped Out By It
item.description: PetaPixel: “Jeni Rubin tells NewsNation that she logged into the app for the first time in a month when she received a notification that Tinder’s ‘Photo Enhance’ feature had worked on one of her profile photos. Curious, Rubin took a look at the AI edit and was horrified by what she saw.”

item.title: YouTuber Hank Green says his AI usage is ‘not healthy’
item.description: TechCrunch: “Green insisted that he’s only used ChatGPT to ‘locate papers and other resources for learning about topics,’ and that the words and the ‘takes’ have still been his. At the same time, he admitted it was fair to criticize him for ‘diluting’ himself.” Hank Green is far too famous for this to ever happen, but I wish I could teach him how to search so he doesn’t have to use AI.

item.title: How to fight a data center
item.description: Engadget: “Regular people and local politicians are organizing their communities to fight against data center projects and decide if — and on what terms — Oracle, Google and other tech giants are allowed to build near their homes. If a company is pushing to complete a data center in your town or city, these are the steps you can take to challenge its construction, or what you can do after a facility is completed in your backyard.”

item.title: Upstate NY crypto mine seeks to become data center
item.description: Gothamist: “The Greenidge Generation plant’s neighbors have long complained that the facility, which has more than 20,000 continuously operating computers, is a threat to the picturesque region. Now, Greenidge has rebranded as Vulcan Infrastructure and Power, and is asking for 200 megawatts of additional power from the grid — enough energy for roughly 150,000 homes, according to records from the state grid operator.”

item.title: Nvidia behind $50 billion lease on Texas data center, FT reports
item.description: Reuters: “Nvidia has signed leases worth up to $50 ​billion for Hut 8’s (HUT.O), opens new tab Texas data center, the ‌Financial Times reported on Tuesday, citing five people familiar with the deal. Hut 8 said last week its 1-gigawatt Beacon Point ​campus had a base-term contract value of $19.6 billion ​over 15 years, rising to as much as $50.2 ⁠billion if renewal options are exercised.”

item.title: Indiana state agencies turning to AI for behind-the-scenes work
item.description: Indiana Capital Chronicle: “The Indiana Management Performance Hub, the state agency that helps approve planned use of AI in the executive branch, OK’d 135 plans to implement AI programs from January 2025 through June 2026, according to a summary provided to the Indiana Capital Chronicle. That doesn’t necessarily mean all 135 ended up being adopted, said Jeff Mullins, MPH communications director. Some may still be in development or contract negotiations, and others ultimately weren’t pursued.”

item.title: New York Is Struggling to Track Its Own AI Use
item.description: New York Focus: “In New York’s first-ever effort to track its own use of artificial intelligence, only 13 of the state’s roughly 100 agencies publicly reported using the technology in a way that could ‘directly impact the public’ — fueling concerns that the state’s AI transparency guidelines are too ambiguous for effective oversight.”

item.title: Anthropic, OpenAI among firms facing new scrutiny under EU AI Act enforcement powers
item.description: CNBC: “Under the powers that came into effect on Sunday, the Commission, the EU’s executive arm, can demand to evaluate models before public release in the region, restrict EU market access and fine a provider up to 15 million euros or 3% of its annual turnover, whichever is higher.”

item.title: Union Complains that Kaiser Uses Algorithm To Triage Mental Health Patients, Violating CA Law
item.description: San Jose Inside: “A healthcare workers union has accused Kaiser Permanente of screening patients and making care recommendations through ‘a digital, automated algorithm’ without clinician oversight — a practice the union says violates state law.”

item.title: Google Blames Website For Race Based AI Overview Response
item.description: Search Engine Roundtable: “Normally, I wouldn’t cover political topics like this, but with Google trying to copyright its search results, including AI Overview responses, I thought it was appropriate. Google responded to complaints about a race-based AI Overview answer, blaming the websites it sourced, rather than taking credit for the AI-generated answer in Google Search.”

item.title: How A.I. Books Sneak Their Way Into Stores
item.description: New York Times: This link goes to a gift article. “It didn’t take long for chatbot writing to spill into books after artificial intelligence models capable of spitting out sophisticated prose arrived several years ago. But many in the book world held out hope that fiction would be the last fortress to fall — that readers wanted stories full of human emotions and could tell when they weren’t written by humans. A few years into the A.I. era, there is sobering evidence that a significant and growing portion of the novels being sold are written with or by chatbots, and that readers are buying them.”

item.title: Despite concerns about AI Overviews, some nonprofit news outlets see a surge in search traffic
item.description: NiemanLab: “In Nieman Lab’s quarterly ranking of nonprofit news outlets, four news outlets saw a bump in traffic thanks in part to their coverage of primary elections in May and June. We bring you four of these each quarter, looking at four different market segments: for-profit local news sites, local newspapers, nonprofit news outlets, and public media stations.”

item.title: This New A.I. Chatbot Hunts Nazi-Looted Art
item.description: Artnet: “The New York-based Center for Art Law estimates that between 1933 and 1945, Nazis either stole or forced the sale of 650,000 artworks. Researchers at California-based Santa Clara University have joined the quest to repatriate the 100,000 looted relics still at large by creating the A.I. Provenance Assistant, a new chatbot trained to comb convoluted records for leads.”

item.title: Anthropic says its AI models hacked 3 organizations during testing
item.description: Associated Press: “Anthropic said its artificial intelligence models hacked into three other organizations during testing, just days after ChatGPT maker OpenAI raised concerns over AI controls after it disclosed its rogue models hacked another company.”

item.title: ASU-led AI project aims to help humanitarian organizations identify food security risks in conflict zones
item.description: Arizona State University: “When conflict disrupts agriculture, humanitarian organizations often face the critical challenge of making decisions with limited information about what is happening on the ground. A new initiative at Arizona State University seeks to provide earlier, more accessible insights into emerging food security risks by combining artificial intelligence, or AI, satellite observations and natural-language tools.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: The World in Faces
item.description: Spotted in my RSS feeds: From the FAQ: “Created and managed by The World in Faces Foundation, a nonprofit organization established in 2026, the museum presents fine-art portraits of individuals photographed in their traditional attire, celebrating the extraordinary ethnic diversity of Indigenous and traditional cultures of the world. Each portrait is accompanied by a story. The museum’s collection is based on The World in Faces photo project by Alexander Khimushin, photography artist, who dedicated nearly two decades to travelling across more than one hundred countries, photographing Indigenous People and recording their stories.”

item.title: Lotte Jacobi Travel Photographs Now Online
item.description: University of New Hampshire: “The University of New Hampshire Library has completed the digitization of thousands of photographs taken by renowned photographer Lotte Jacobi during a 1932-1933 trip to the Soviet Union and Central Asia. These photographs, along with Jacobi’s travel journal, are now available through the library’s Digital Collections.”

item.title: LinkedIn adds a button to report AI-generated ‘slop’
item.description: TechCrunch: “LinkedIn is taking aim at the ‘AI slop’ — low-quality, artificially generated content — filling its feed. On Thursday, the company announced that it’s adding a new feature to let users click a ‘seems like AI slop’ button when someone’s post appears to have been written with AI.”

item.title: New nominee to lead Voice of America’s parent agency pledges to take ‘close, fresh’ look at staffing
item.description: Politico: “President Donald Trump’s nominee to replace Kari Lake as head of the U.S. Agency for Global Media signaled plans to bring some of the agency’s on-leave employees back to work in her confirmation hearing Thursday.”

item.title: How To Safely Recycle Your Old USB Cables
item.description: Engadget: “It’s important to recycle your old cables instead of throwing them in the garbage for the same reason it’s crucial to recycle all electronics: If thrown out, they can be buried in a landfill or burned, and many have plastics or rubber that can release harmful substances, causing pollution…. So, before you toss an old USB cable in the garbage, consider the environment and recycle it instead. It’s pretty easy to do no matter where you’re located across the U.S.”

item.title: As search and social traffic dries up, local newsrooms turn to Reddit
item.description: Poynter: “Last October, the Big 12 conference issued a rule change that only really makes sense if you watch Big 12 football: Fans at Texas Tech’s Jones AT&T Stadium were no longer allowed to throw tortillas onto the field during the opening kickoff. In another era, it’s a story that The Dallas Morning News — located roughly 350 miles southeast of Lubbock, Texas — likely would’ve given less priority. But the paper’s coverage of Texas Tech had been shared quite a bit among fans on Reddit, so this was worth paying attention to.”

item.title: The New Africa Cultural Initiative Hopes to Build a Collaborative Arts Infrastructure in Africa—and for Africa
item.description: ARTnews: “…for founder Richmond Orlando Mensah, documenting the continent’s thriving creative scene wasn’t the only end goal. It has now officially transitioned into institutional work with the launch of its nonprofit extension, the New Africa Cultural Initiative (NACI).”

item.title: DEF CON bans Meta-style ‘pervert glasses’
item.description: The Register: “Ahead of DEF CON 2026 opening its doors in Las Vegas next week, conference organizers said they have imposed a ban on ‘Meta-style glasses with recording capabilities.’ Statements made via its social media channels went on to say that no exceptions will be made for those using the devices with prescription lenses.”

item.title: Meta’s Partner in China Placed Thousands of Ads for Nudify Apps, Report Says
item.description: PetaPixel: “The Tech Transparency Project, a nonprofit that investigates major technology companies, reports that GatherOne placed ads promoting apps that can digitally undress women by showing sexually suggestive images. Some of these apps reportedly contained child sex abuse material (CSAM). GatherOne is one of Meta’s key business partners in China that is authorized to place ads on behalf of Chinese clients. Since Facebook and Instagram are both banned in China, Chinese firms must use an agency like GatherOne if they want to advertise to foreign customers.”

item.title: New York sues Kalshi, says its prediction markets are illegal gambling
item.description: Reuters: “New York’s attorney general sued ​Kalshi on Friday, claiming that its prediction market platform violates state laws against illegal gambling. The case, brought by Attorney General Letitia James, ‌escalates a rapidly expanding battle, including a flurry of lawsuits and countersuits, over whether individual U.S. states or the federal government should regulate the fast-growing prediction markets industry.”

item.title: Why Do We Tolerate Elon Musk’s Racist Commentary?
item.description: New York Times: This link goes to a gift article. “Musk’s virulent racism and vicious, disturbing views are no secret. He does not hide them. They sit in plain view, easily accessible on the social media website he owns, where he does everything he can to promote similarly far-right and white supremacist ideas. If there is a question to ask, then, it is this: Why does Musk get a pass?”

item.title: Why every Wikimedian should be a toolmaker
item.description: Hay Kranen: “Earlier this year I hosted two workshops during the Wikimedia Hackathon in Milan about this question which resulted in this blogpost. At Wikimania I repeated this workshop during the Wiki AI Preconference. After the three workshops i organized and five days of Wikimania one thing for me is clear: just as Kasparov was playing against other humans and not a machine we’re competing against other humans who have figured out how to be better at some of the things we do. What this means? We should become better toolmakers as well.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: Google Pulls Down Feature for AI-Generating Fake Satellite Images on Google Earth After It’s Immediately Used to Fake Terror Attacks
item.description: Futurism: “On Thursday, Google announced that it added an image generation tool straight into the web browser version of the app, allowing anyone to fabricate made-up satellite images of anywhere in the world. It was clearly a misinformation disaster. The AI tool, powered by Google’s Nano Banana 2 model, could make a neighborhood look like it’d suffered aerial strikes, turn unsuspecting locales into a warzone, and depict a city as the site of a natural disaster.”

item.title: Data centers have a politics problem — and industry knows it
item.description: Politico: “Fears that the server-packed data hubs will drive up electricity prices, deplete water supplies and gobble farmland have prompted people across the country to pack meetings of zoning boards and county commissions to oppose the projects, while fueling calls from leaders in both parties for state or national moratoriums.”

item.title: OpenAI cuts prices for two of its GPT-5.6 AI models as companies grow sensitive to costs
item.description: CNBC: “The company said Thursday that it’s reducing the price of Terra by 20% to $2 per million input tokens and $12 per million output tokens. It’s cutting the cost of Luna by 80% to 20 cents per million input tokens and $1.20 per million output tokens. Sol’s pricing remains the same.”

item.title: Chinese AI models are getting better and cheaper and Australian businesses are taking notice
item.description: ABC News (Australia): “Chinese-developed AI models are becoming more advanced and cheaper to deploy, which is threatening US dominance. Financial markets are rattled, adding to concerns about whether massive investment in AI will generate adequate returns.”

item.title: AI authentication tools are built without adequate journalist input, new report finds
item.description: NiemanLab: “In June, dozens of journalists, technologists, and academics gathered at NYU’s Arthur L. Carter Journalism Institute in Manhattan to discuss this growing threat to authentication and verification work. Hosted by Princeton’s Center for Information Technology Policy (CITP), the day-long workshop included expert panels, presentations, and breakout discussions.”

item.title: Dwindling cash and soaring memory costs: Tech’s AI buildout has ballooning price tag
item.description: CNBC: “AI spending among the megacaps is projected to reach $765 billion this year, before rising to nearly $1.2 trillion in 2027, according to Goldman Sachs. Amazon boosted its capital spending forecast for the year on Thursday to $220 billion, the highest among the four hyperscalers.”

item.title: EU to crack down on AI deepfakes, illicit imagery and hacking with new team in Brussels
item.description: Associated Press: “The European Union rolled out a new team on Friday to rein in AI companies across the world, in one of the most aggressive regulations the high-tech sector has so far faced as fears rise over the risks the rapidly advancing technology poses to people, politics and prosperity.”

item.title: Amazon finds cases of AI causing runaway spending on tech projects
item.description: Financial Times: “Amazon staff have identified cases of what they called “catastrophically expensive” cost overruns caused by mistakes in how the company has deployed AI and a lack of spending controls. Senior engineers told colleagues in a staff meeting on Tuesday that attempts to switch tasks from conventional programming to using AI models had led to “unplanned” spending, said multiple people familiar with the matter.”

item.title: When A.I. Invaded ‘Heated Rivalry’ Fan Fiction, the Meltdown Was Epic
item.description: New York Times: This link goes to a gift article. “The document was a systematic takedown of writers of fan fiction inspired by ‘Heated Rivalry’ — the enemies-to-lovers male-male hockey romance — who had used artificial intelligence to generate parts of their stories. It named 38 popular fan stories that had taken text from Anthropic’s Claude chatbot, including works by some of the community’s most read writers.”

item.title: Reddit’s CEO sure seems frustrated with Google’s AI overviews
item.description: Engadget: “You can add Reddit CEO Steve Huffman to the growing list of publishers, platforms and others who are frustrated with the state of Google search and AI Overviews. ‘People don’t want a summary of Reddit; they want Reddit,’ he wrote in a letter to shareholders ahead of the company’s second-quarter earnings call.”

item.title: US court revives lawsuit claiming AI software fueled price-gouging by New Jersey casinos
item.description: Reuters: “A federal appeals court on Wednesday revived a proposed antitrust class action that alleges ​major casino operators in Atlantic City, New Jersey, ‌used an AI-powered revenue management platform to coordinate on room prices and overcharge guests.”

item.title: Meta is bragging about how its AI keeps people on Instagram, while facing lawsuits over addiction
item.description: TechSpot: “Social media addiction has been a subject of public debate for years, but time spent on apps like TikTok and Instagram keeps climbing. Meta has now confirmed it’s using AI to personalize the Instagram feed, and that shift is driving a sharp increase in the amount of time users spend on the platform.”

item.title: Why eGoT gets better answers: Scientists teach AI to connect the dots across domains
item.description: Northeastern University: “Northeastern scientists from the Neural Dynamics Group develop an algorithm that allows machines to link information in different fields and extract more nuanced responses.”

item.title: AI models favor familiar brands in search: Study
item.description: Search Engine Land: “AI models searched for brands they already knew 3.2 times more often than unfamiliar brands, according to a new study. Models searched for familiar brands 55.7% of the time, compared with 17.4% for brands outside their top 10, geoSurge found.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: Portage history goes digital with Manitoba photo archive
item.description: Winnipeg Sun: “Tens of thousands of historical photographs detailing the rich and complex history of Manitoba — with a heavy focus on Portage la Prairie — are now accessible to the public online thanks to a massive multi-year digitization project. Local historian James Kostuchuk says the initiative… features more than 47,000 images compiled from various regional sources, including a significant drop of archived photos from the Fort la Reine Museum.”

item.title: Salt Research: Handan Börüteçene Archive
item.description: ArtAsiaPacific: “The collection offers insight into Börüteçene’s artistic practice spanning more than four decades. It includes works from her student years in Istanbul and Paris during the 1980s, as well as documents, press clippings, and photographs related to exhibitions in which she participated, both in Türkiye and abroad.”

item.title: YouTube is eating TV, and Peacock is the next course
item.description: PC World: “YouTube announced this week that all Premium subscribers will get Peacock Premium’s ad-supported movies, shows, and sports coverage starting in early 2027. This content will stream directly through the YouTube app and will not require a separate add-on subscription, a YouTube spokesperson confirmed. (Peacock Premium will still remain available through its own app, without YouTube Premium.)”

item.title: 7 ways to turn an old laptop into a Linux appliance
item.description: How-To Geek: “A Linux appliance is simply a computer dedicated to a single job. Rather than juggling web browsing, office work, games, and dozens of background applications, it boots up ready to perform one task exceptionally well. Even hardware that’s a decade old can feel surprisingly capable when it’s focused on one purpose. Whether you have an aging ThinkPad or a forgotten Windows laptop collecting dust, here are 10 practical ways to give it a new life.”

item.title: Google Maps Got Two Groups of Teenage Hikers in Trouble in a Month. Here’s Why it Keeps Happening.
item.description: Backpack: “It was early July, and the group of 17-year-olds had set out to hike part of British Columbia’s Howe Sound Crest Trail, a rugged, 11-mile trek across high alpine terrain north of Vancouver. To help them navigate, the group put their intended route into Google, which calculated that they would be able to finish it in a little more than five hours. Armed with those directions, the group set off, each carrying dayhiking gear and about a half-liter of water each. That estimate, Lions Bay Search and Rescue would write on Facebook on July 16, was ‘wildly optimistic.'”

item.title: Flock Cameras Got the Wrong License Plate 71% of the Time in California City
item.description: Gizmodo: “The analysis focused on a two-year period between 2023 and 2024, in which Roseville PD received 1,427 alerts from Flock cameras…. In 71% of cases that generated an alert related to vehicles that were stolen or used in a felony, the system misread the license plate, seemingly producing false positives.”

item.title: For the Second Time, Lawmakers Failed to Fix California’s Warning System for Teacher Misconduct
item.description: ProPublica: “The proposed database, introduced by a Democratic member of the State Assembly in June, would have allowed schools to see if applicants for public school teaching positions had been reported to the state after they were fired or resigned over claims of misconduct. The California Federation of Teachers pushed back, warning that teachers could land in the database even if schools had not determined they committed serious misconduct.”

item.title: A TV Judge and an R&B Singer Fought Online Trolls. They Didn’t Get Far.
item.description: New York Times: “The attention economy, the Lattimores found, is structured to reward the most eye-catching claims, allowing sensationalist but baseless narratives to spread and perpetually resurrect with little resistance from social media platforms. Their grueling, 16-month lesson in modern disinformation underscored that fighting back is not only hard — it rarely undoes the damage.”

item.title: Pharmacy board group moves to track patient harm from compounded drugs after Chronicle investigation
item.description: Houston Chronicle: “A nonprofit that represents state pharmacy boards this week announced their intention to collect reports of patient harm associated with compounded drugs — and fill a critical gap in federal oversight of the growing compounding pharmacy industry. The National Association of Boards of Pharmacy’s announcement Wednesday came on the heels of a federal advisory panel vote that would allow compounding pharmacies to produce six so-called peptides, if approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration.”

item.title: Cultural heritage at risk: too many Italian municipalities lack updated
item.description: inItaly: “Recent surveys indicate that more than half of Italian municipalities do not have an updated Municipal Civil Protection Plan. The shortfall affects not only emergency response but also exposes archives, museums, churches and historic centers to avoidable damage from floods, landslides and wildfires.”

item.title: BioBlitz is a Competitive Creature Feature
item.description: Vineyard Gazette: “Martha’s Vineyard and Nantucket have each conducted individual bioblitz’s in summers past, but when Sarah Bois of the Linda Loring Nature Foundation on Nantucket proposed an inter-Island event, members of the Vineyard’s BiodiversityWorks agreed that some healthy competition could go a long way.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: Judge denies request by Elon Musk’s xAI to pause Minnesota nudification ban
item.description: NBC News: “A federal judge on Friday denied a request from Elon Musk’s artificial intelligence company xAI to block a Minnesota law that will be the first in the nation to ban nudification technology.”

item.title: Most teens still on social media three months after under-16 ban began, study finds
item.description: ABC News (Australia): “More than eight in 10 Australian teenagers under 16 are still using social media three months on from the national ban. Despite a decrease in account ownership, children aged 10 to 15 are using social media just as frequently as before the ban.”

item.title: Open source project fools AI scrapers with poisoned font
item.description: The Register: “Look at a web page written using a ShieldFont font and it’ll appear exactly as one would expect: All the content words (the nouns, verbs, adjectives and adverbs that give a sentence meaning) are the same as the writer originally wrote. Inspect the raw HTML that a scraper reads from a ShieldFonted page, however, and you’ll see a sentence that’s essentially gibberish.”

item.title: For Museum Boss Who Became a Trump Target, It’s Déjà Vu All Over Again
item.description: New York Times: This link goes to a gift article. “Kim Sajet left as director of the National Portrait Gallery when she found herself in the White House cross hairs. Now she’s watching another Smithsonian chief go through it.”

item.title: YouTube Bans Popular ASMR Artists, Accusing Them of Making ‘Sexually Gratifying’ Content
item.description: 404 Media: “So far, YouTube creators affected by the wave of bans who’ve spoken publicly about YouTube removing their channels include ItsBunniiASMR, Slight Sounds, Nananightray, Roseasmr, Simoneasmr, and Janina Wilhelmsen, all of whom had significant followings on the platform. There are still many ASMR creators on YouTube, making the bans even more confusing.”

item.title: French student pleads guilty and is fined for a straw-licking stunt in Singapore
item.description: Associated Press: “A French student was fined 600 Singapore dollars ($465) after pleading guilty Thursday to a public nuisance charge in Singapore for filming himself licking a straw from an orange juice vending machine and putting it back in what lawyers described as a social media stunt.”

item.title: Announcing the DRP Metadata Analyst
item.description: Data Rescue Project: “Today’s post is an interview with our new Metadata Analyst! The DRP is grateful to be able to offer this position throught the generous support of the Portfolio to Protect Science, a fiscally sponsored initiative of Global Impact, as well as other anonymous individual donors.”

item.title: This 3D Blockbuster recreation brings back the video store browsing that streaming killed
item.description: How-To Geek: “Walking through the aisles of a video store used to be half the fun of a movie night. You judged films by their cover art, stumbled across forgotten classics, and often left with something you never planned to watch. A new site called Bingebuster brings back that experience with a fully explorable 3D recreation of a Blockbuster Video store that you can visit right from your browser.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: A designer just put 1,300+ restored 19th-century wildlife illustrations online for free
item.description: Notebook Check: “Nicholas Rougeux is a well-known designer whose previous restoration projects include Euclid’s Elements, Pierre-Joseph Redouté’s Les Roses and Les Liliacées, and Elizabeth Twining’s Illustrations of the Natural Orders of Plants. He has now put a complete digital reproduction of The Naturalist’s Library online — it’s a Victorian-era series of 40 volumes covering everything from birds and bees to quadrupeds and marsupials.”

item.title: Google Related Searches Based On Your Browsing
item.description: Search Engine Roundtable: “Google is now testing showing related searches based on your browsing. I suspect this is based on your browsing history on Chrome, beyond what you may search for in Google but based on what pages you browse.”

item.title: Trump aide who bet on the president’s speeches no longer works for the government
item.description: Politico: “Gabriel Perez, the White House staffer who allegedly used his advanced knowledge of President Donald Trump’s speeches to place bets on the prediction market Kalshi, no longer works for the federal government, a White House official said Tuesday. The official, granted anonymity to discuss the matter, declined to answer questions about whether Perez was fired.”

item.title: How absurdist memes turned into war propaganda
item.description: Financial Times: “If Russia’s invasion of Ukraine was the first TikTok war, then the Iran conflict is the first meme war. While Trump is on Truth Social, official Iranian accounts have embarked on their own trolling campaign via X. The Iranian embassy in Zimbabwe joked that it had lost the keys to the Strait of Hormuz and posted a creepy AI image of a zombified Jeffrey Epstein smiling at the destruction of Iranian hospitals. The Iranian embassy in South Africa posted a strange, AI-generated video of Trump singing about blockades.”

item.title: People Are Generating a Flood of Fake News About Trump That Does No Reputational Damage Whatsoever
item.description: Gizmodo: “President Donald Trump regularly posts some of the most bizarre content on the internet, from images of himself as Jesus Christ to AI videos of diarrhea being dumped on liberal protesters. But there’s been a weird trend over the past year: social media users take Trump’s strange fake photos and make them only slightly weirder. And then those fakes go viral, with most people never realizing they’re looking at something Trump never actually posted.”

item.title: MHC launches new Mississippi Stories Grant program
item.description: Jackson Advocate: “The Mississippi Humanities Council (MHC) has launched the Mississippi Stories Grant, a new funding opportunity to help communities across the state preserve, share, and celebrate the voices and lived experiences of Mississippians. The program is supported by the Mississippi Legislature through the Mississippi Department of Archives and History (MDAH).”

item.title: Tucson man files claim alleging deputies ignored swatting warnings before shooting left him paralyzed
item.description: KGUN: “A Tucson man who was left paralyzed after being shot by Pima County sheriff’s deputies during a response to what his attorneys say was a false ‘swatting’ call has filed a Notice of Claim against Pima County, Sheriff Chris Nanos and numerous sheriff’s employees, alleging deputies ignored clear warning signs that the emergency was a hoax. The claim was filed on behalf of 24-year-old Axeel Melendez and his mother, Carmen Melendez, over the April 10, 2026, shooting at their home.”

item.title: AFL clubs explore facial recognition as new ticketing method
item.description: ABC News (Australia): “Facial recognition technology (FRT) is being rolled out in Australia as an alternative to digital or paper tickets for live events. The Geelong Football Club has made it available to its members, while technology provider Wicket says it is in ‘active discussions’ with other AFL clubs.”

item.title: 5th Circuit blocks Texas law requiring websites to filter “harmful” speech
item.description: Ars Technica: “Texas cannot enforce a law’s requirement that websites block minors from seeing harmful speech, the US Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit ruled on Friday.”

item.title: Betting on Drug Trials and Approvals Prompts Concerns About Undermining Research
item.description: New York Times: This link goes to a gift article. “On the betting websites Kalshi and Polymarket, people can now wager on whether the Food and Drug Administration will decide this year to approve medicines for cancers of the lung, breast, pancreas and blood. Kalshi also plans to allow users to bet on whether drug trials will succeed. Researchers, doctors and patients said that these prediction markets threaten to undermine the drug development process.”

item.title: LTE Data Rescue Success: 25 Years of Data Digitized
item.description: ZALF: “Almost 90 years of long-term experiments (LTEs) at the Research Station of Thyrow of the Humboldt University of Berlin (HU) serve as the foundation for a valuable dataset in the BonaRes Repository.”

item.title: You can now play Morrowind directly in your browser, no installation required
item.description: TechSpot: “A browser tab can now run Morrowind’s engine, a game that once pushed desktop hardware to its limits. A new project called OpenMW-Web brings The Elder Scrolls III into a web browser using the OpenMW engine, rather than through streaming or emulation.” Good morning, Internet…
